paragraphs.context: Everything the dragonets knew about the outside world came from scrolls
paragraphs.mainIdea: All the dragonets knew about the outside world came from scrolls. Their favorite story was about a SeaWing dragonet who ran away and then came home.
paragraphs.simple: Everything the dragonets knew about the outside world came from scrolls. The Talons of Peace had collected these scrolls. Their favorite was The Missing Princess. It was an old story about a SeaWing dragonet who ran away. Her royal family searched the whole ocean for her. At the end she found her way home. Her parents welcomed her with open wings, a feast and joy.

paragraphs.context: There was something not quite right about the littlest dragonet
paragraphs.mainIdea: Sunny is a SandWing, more or less. But her scales are too golden, her eyes are gray-green, and her tail has no poison barb.
paragraphs.simple: Dune was a dragon who had been badly hurt. He taught them how to stay alive. He was a SandWing, and so was Sunny, more or less. Something was not quite right about the littlest dragonet. Her scales were too golden. Her eyes were gray-green and not sparkling black. Worst of all, her tail curled into an ordinary point, like the tails of most dragon tribes. It did not end in the poison barb that was the most dangerous weapon of a SandWing.

paragraphs.context: A real scavenger would be smaller than her, according to this scroll
paragraphs.mainIdea: Starflight says Clay is twice Sunny’s size, and a real scavenger would be smaller than her. He tells what the scrolls say about scavengers.
paragraphs.simple: ‘That is hardly fair,’ said Starflight. ‘He is twice Sunny’s size. A real scavenger would be smaller than her, says this scroll over here. It says that scavengers have no scales, no wings and no tail. They walk on two legs, which sounds very unsteady to me. I bet they fall over all the time. They like treasure almost as much as dragons do. The scrolls say scavengers attack dragons that are alone, and steal —’

paragraphs.context: Morrowseer was even bigger than Kestrel, and five times more terrifying
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morrowseer is even bigger than Kestrel and five times more scary. He looks down at the dragonets lined up in front of him.
paragraphs.simple: Morrowseer was even bigger than Kestrel, and five times more scary. He spread his wings, which had rough, sharp edges and were like a bat’s. He looked down at the dragonets lined up in front of him. He had silver scales like stars on the underside of his wings, as Starflight did. But on him they seemed to shine from very far away and gave off a cold light.

paragraphs.context: The Talons of Peace need you to survive long enough to fulfill the prophecy
paragraphs.mainIdea: Webs says all of this is for the dragonets’ safety. The Talons of Peace need them to live long enough to make the prophecy come true, and many dragons would love to catch them.
paragraphs.simple: ‘This is for your safety,’ said Webs, cutting in. His voice was softer than Kestrel’s, but Clay could tell he was angry from the way his long blue-green tail hit the floor. ‘That is what all of this is for. The Talons of Peace need you to live long enough to make the prophecy come true. You have no idea how many dragons would love to catch you five.’

paragraphs.context: Without Tsunami’s glow-in-the-dark scales to guide him
paragraphs.mainIdea: Clay jumps into the river and swims against the current to the rock wall. Without Tsunami’s glow-in-the-dark scales to guide him, it takes longer to find the gap to the other cave.
paragraphs.simple: He ran over to the river and jumped in. Through the water he could hear the soft echo of Sunny’s nervous squeak as he swam against the current to the rock wall. He did not have Tsunami’s glow-in-the-dark scales to guide him, so it took longer than usual to find the gap that led through to the other cave. But at last he felt open space under his claws, and he ducked down and squeezed through.

paragraphs.context: He had never actually tried holding his breath for an entire hour before
paragraphs.mainIdea: Clay’s chest begins to hurt as he swims in the dark. He has never tried to hold his breath for a whole hour, and he starts to worry.
paragraphs.simple: He did not know how long he swam through the dark, twisting channel. But after a while his chest began to hurt. He had never really tried holding his breath for a whole hour before. The dragonets only knew he could do it because a couple of scrolls said so about MudWings. What if it took practice? What if only full-grown MudWings could do it? What if his lungs were still too small?

paragraphs.context: He dug his claws into the rock and hung on for dear life
paragraphs.mainIdea: Clay holds on tight to the rock. His skin hurts badly from the poison, and he cannot stand to think how far Tsunami may have fallen.
paragraphs.simple: He dug his claws into the rock and held on with all his strength, as if his life depended on it. He shut his eyes tight, even though the darkness was already dark enough. His skin, full of poison, hurt terribly as it stretched under his scales. He could not stand to think of how far Tsunami might have fallen. He could picture her broken body somewhere far below him.

paragraphs.context: Wind whistled past his face — wind! He’d imagined it all wrong
paragraphs.mainIdea: Clay dives toward her and feels the wind. It is not what he had imagined. It feels like a living thing that fights him.
paragraphs.simple: Clay turned into a dive and shot down toward her. He held his wings close to his body and fought back the fear as he dropped fast. Wind whistled past his face. Wind! He had imagined it all wrong. It was like a living thing. It grabbed his tail to throw him off balance. It flew into his eyes to blind him. It pushed up under his wings to slow him down. It seemed to dig claws as sharp as ice into his skin, cutting in under his scales.

paragraphs.context: She glared at Tsunami. “Nobody touches my treasure.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: The orange dragon grabs Tsunami’s talon and squeezes it hard. She says that nobody touches her treasure.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Oh, neither do I,’ said the orange dragon. ‘That is why it makes me so sad when trouble keeps coming to me.’ She reached out and grabbed Tsunami’s talon, with the medallion still in it, and squeezed hard. Clay started forward, but the strange dragon shot a bolt of flame at him, so he had to duck back. She glared at Tsunami. ‘Nobody touches my treasure.’

paragraphs.context: She’d held on to her power for thirty years, despite fourteen brave
paragraphs.mainIdea: Queen Scarlet is smaller than Clay expected, but she is a deadly queen who has kept her power for thirty years. She is allied with Burn, who hated the prophecy.
paragraphs.simple: She was smaller than he had expected, smaller than Kestrel. But Clay knew they should not think too little of the SkyWing queen. She had held on to her power for thirty years, even with fourteen brave, foolish challengers. They were all dead now. She was one of the longest-living and deadliest queens in Pyrrhia. She would also be one of the worst dragons to get her claws on the dragonets of destiny, especially because she was allied with Burn. Burn hated the prophecy and had destroyed the SkyWing egg six years ago.

paragraphs.context: Queen Scarlet’s vast palace was carved into the gray-and-black rocks
paragraphs.mainIdea: From his tower, Clay can see the SkyWing kingdom. Queen Scarlet’s huge palace is cut into the rocks of the peak, half inside the mountain and half open to the sky.
paragraphs.simple: At the bottom of his tower there was only bare rock. But from up here he could see the heart of the SkyWing kingdom stretched across the top of the mountain. Queen Scarlet’s huge palace was cut into the gray-and-black rocks of the peak. Half of it was inside tunnels and caves, and the other half was open to the sky and full of defenses. Fire-colored dragons crawled across the mountain face, digging and blasting out new parts of the palace. They were covered in stone dust and dirt, and they looked no brighter than MudWings.

paragraphs.context: He’d never heard of dragons setting other dragons on fire just by touching them
paragraphs.mainIdea: Horizon’s tail hits Peril’s scales and bursts into flames. Clay has never seen or heard of a dragon setting another dragon on fire just by touching.
paragraphs.simple: Peril whirled around, away from his claws, and knocked him down to the sand. His tail, with its barb, bounced off her scales with a spark like tiny lightning, and then burst into flames. Fire covered the poisoned tip, and Horizon howled in pain. Clay had never seen anything like it. He had never heard of dragons setting other dragons on fire just by touching them.

paragraphs.context: I was born with too much fire
paragraphs.mainIdea: Peril tells Clay why no one else wants her: she was born with too much fire. Queen Scarlet saved her and killed her mother to punish her.
paragraphs.simple: ‘No one else wants me,’ said Peril, in a calm, plain voice. ‘No one can even touch me. You saw that. I was born with too much fire. Usually when dragons like me hatch, the SkyWings drop them off the highest mountain peak. That is what my mother was going to do. But Queen Scarlet saved me and killed her, to punish her.’ Her eyes went cold at the words my mother.

paragraphs.context: Something — someone else — had killed Fjord for him
paragraphs.mainIdea: Fjord is dead, but Clay did not win fairly and did not want him to die. Clay feels very guilty about Fjord, Dune and his friends.
paragraphs.simple: He had not won in a fair way. He had not found the strength in himself to kill. He had not even wanted Fjord to die. Something, or someone else, had killed Fjord for him. And still there was a ball of twisting guilt in his stomach. He felt guilty about Fjord, about Dune, about Glory’s strange drugged state, and about Sunny, wherever she was. He felt guilty about Starflight, who would never live through the arena, and about Tsunami, who might, but only if she did not get herself killed first doing crazy things.

paragraphs.context: If he could just get her attention … if he could only talk to
paragraphs.mainIdea: Clay hopes to get Peril’s attention. He hopes she can find a way to save the prisoners while the soldiers are at a feast for Burn.
paragraphs.simple: Clay looked around. Most of the prisoners were curled up to sleep for the night. It was only sunset, but there was not much else to do up on the rock columns. There were no guards in sight. There must be some kind of welcome feast for Burn. He hoped all the SkyWing soldiers would be there, eating and making bets on the gladiator fights planned for tomorrow. And he hoped Peril would be in her room, the cave closest to the arena. If he could just get her attention, if he could only talk to her, maybe she would find a way to save them.

paragraphs.context: We have a full slate of thrilling games today, so let’s begin!
paragraphs.mainIdea: Vermilion tells the crowd to begin the games. Then Tsunami breaks away from her guards and charges at him, and he shoots into the sky in terror.
paragraphs.simple: Vermilion flew down to the middle of the arena. ‘Fellow dragons,’ he called. ‘Loyal SkyWings, visiting MudWings and honored SandWing guests. We have a full list of exciting games today, so let us begin!’ He turned to point at Tsunami just as she broke away from her guards and charged at him. He cried out in terror and shot into the sky. He barely got away from her claws.

paragraphs.context: I thought I was born a killer, but it turns out I wasn’t
paragraphs.mainIdea: Peril says she thought she was born a killer, but Queen Scarlet made her one, or she let herself become one. She says Clay was born a killer and chose to be something else.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Only because of you.’ She shook her head. ‘I thought I was born a killer, but it turns out I was not. Queen Scarlet made me that way, or I let myself become that way. It is like I chose it without knowing I chose it. But you were born that way.’ Clay winced, and he felt the other dragonets staring at him. ‘You knew what you were like, and you chose to be something else. I feel that I cannot be one of you unless I can do that, too.’

paragraphs.context: We have breeding night once a month and then everyone goes back
paragraphs.mainIdea: Cattail laughs because Clay knows nothing about MudWings. She does not know who his father was, and she says his father does not care.
paragraphs.simple: Cattail threw her head back and laughed. It was a high croaking sound, like a thousand bullfrogs yelling at once. ‘You really do not know anything about MudWings, do you?’ she said when she could catch her breath again. ‘I do not even know who your father was. And he certainly does not care. We have breeding night once a month, and then everyone goes back to their own sleephouses. No, dear, there is no father here for you.’

paragraphs.context: MudWing dragons laid their eggs in warm mud nests protected by walls
paragraphs.mainIdea: Clay is told how MudWings keep their eggs safe in warm mud nests. The firstborn helps the other dragonets out of their eggs.
paragraphs.simple: They told him that MudWing dragons laid their eggs in warm mud nests, protected by walls of hot rocks. The eggs were so safe that the mother never needed to check on them. The dragonets were usually born when she was not even there. The firstborn was always the biggest. His or her first job was to help the other dragonets out of their eggs by cracking the shells from the outside.

sentences.context: because he was paying attention to his friends instead of watching for feathers
sentences.simple: He kept losing chickens during hunting practice because he was paying attention to his friends and not watching for feathers.
sentences.grammar: ‘instead of + -ing’ (instead of watching) means he did one thing and not the other; ‘because he was paying attention’ gives the reason.

sentences.context: Thinking about what he’d nearly done to his friends made him feel
sentences.simple: When he thought about what he had almost done to his friends, he felt as if all his fire had been taken out of him.
sentences.grammar: ‘Thinking about ...’ is an -ing phrase used as the subject; ‘what he’d nearly done’ is a clause with past perfect (he had almost done it earlier); ‘had been sucked out’ is passive.

sentences.context: a runaway SeaWing dragonet whose royal family tore up the whole ocean
sentences.simple: Their favorite was The Missing Princess, an old story about a SeaWing dragonet who ran away. Her royal family searched the whole ocean for her.
sentences.grammar: ‘whose royal family’ means ‘the dragonet’s royal family’; ‘tore up the whole ocean looking for her’ means they searched everywhere very hard.

sentences.context: Which opponent would you prefer, the stunted SandWing or the lazy RainWing?
sentences.simple: Which one would you rather fight: the SandWing who did not grow well, or the lazy RainWing?
sentences.grammar: ‘Which opponent would you prefer’ asks about a choice (would + prefer); the two choices come after the comma, joined by ‘or’.

sentences.context: It says that scavengers have no scales, no wings, and no tail
sentences.simple: It says that scavengers have no scales, wings or tail. They walk on two legs, which Starflight thinks sounds unsteady.
sentences.grammar: ‘no scales, no wings, and no tail’ repeats ‘no’ in a list; ‘which sounds very unstable to me’ is a ‘which’ clause about the whole idea ‘they walk on two legs’.

sentences.context: Dune, the maimed dragon who taught them survival skills, was a SandWing
sentences.simple: Dune was a dragon who had been hurt badly. He taught them how to stay alive. He was a SandWing, and so was Sunny, more or less.
sentences.grammar: ‘so was Sunny’ means ‘Sunny was a SandWing too’ (so + verb + subject); ‘the maimed dragon who taught them survival skills’ gives extra information about Dune.

sentences.context: instead of ending with the poisonous barb that was a SandWing’s most dangerous weapon
sentences.simple: Worst of all, her tail curled into an ordinary point, like the tails of most dragon tribes. It did not end in the poison barb that was a SandWing’s most dangerous weapon.
sentences.grammar: ‘instead of + -ing’ means ‘not this, but that’: her tail did not end with a barb; the ‘that’ clause tells which barb; ‘most dangerous’ is a superlative.

sentences.context: Because Burn is bigger and scarier and could crush her like a bug
sentences.simple: Burn is bigger and scarier. She could crush Blaze like a bug if they really fought claw to claw.
sentences.grammar: ‘Because’ answers the question ‘why’; ‘could crush ... if they actually fought’ is a ‘what if’ sentence (could + if + past) about something that has not happened.

sentences.context: Glory fell asleep every day, usually after lunch, for a couple of hours
sentences.simple: Glory fell asleep every day, usually after lunch, for a couple of hours. But Clay had expected her to stay awake while Morrowseer was around.
sentences.grammar: ‘had expected her to stay awake’ (past perfect) shows what Clay thought earlier; ‘expect someone to + verb’ means to think they will do it.

sentences.context: as if his scales were being slowly peeled off, one by one
sentences.simple: He felt the same way, frozen in place, as if his scales were being slowly pulled off, one by one, while the giant NightWing looked closely at them.
sentences.grammar: ‘as if ... were being peeled’ is passive and continuous; it tells how it felt, not what was true.

sentences.context: Shudders of horror were running through Clay so violently
sentences.simple: Clay shook so much with fear that he was afraid one of the big dragons would see the waves on the water.
sentences.grammar: ‘so violently that he was afraid ...’ shows a result; ‘were running’ is the past continuous for something going on at that moment.

sentences.context: Without Tsunami’s glow-in-the-dark scales to guide him
sentences.simple: He did not have Tsunami’s glow-in-the-dark scales to guide him, so it took longer than usual to find the gap that led through to the other cave.
sentences.grammar: ‘Without + noun’ means ‘not having it’; ‘scales to guide him’ uses ‘to + verb’ for the job of the scales; ‘that led through’ is a ‘that’ clause telling which gap.

sentences.context: You can only hold your breath for an hour — you could get trapped
sentences.simple: You can hold your breath for only an hour. You could get trapped with no air and drown.
sentences.grammar: ‘get trapped’ is a ‘get’ passive (like ‘be trapped’); ‘could’ shows a danger that is possible; ‘with no air’ tells the condition.

sentences.context: The dragonets only knew he could because that’s what it said about MudWings
sentences.simple: The dragonets only knew he could hold his breath for an hour because a couple of scrolls said so about MudWings.
sentences.grammar: ‘he could’ leaves out ‘hold his breath for an hour’ because it was just said; ‘only ... because’ gives the one reason for what the dragonets thought.

sentences.context: He felt the mud squelch into the gaps between his scales
sentences.simple: He felt the mud push into the gaps between his scales with a wet sound. He realized that the pain from the cave poison was fading, as if the mud was healing him.
sentences.grammar: ‘felt the mud squelch’ = ‘felt’ + object + verb without ‘to’; ‘as if the mud was healing him’ tells how it seemed.

sentences.context: especially since she was allied with Burn, who hated the prophecy
sentences.simple: She would be one of the worst dragons to get her claws on the dragonets of destiny, especially because she was allied with Burn. Burn hated the prophecy and had destroyed the SkyWing egg six years ago.
sentences.grammar: ‘especially since’ means ‘especially because’; ‘who hated ... and had destroyed’ is a ‘who’ clause, and ‘had destroyed’ (past perfect) is the earlier action.

sentences.context: if he relaxed and just looked, he could see how things should fit together
sentences.simple: He had the same funny feeling that he had when he looked at Tsunami’s crooked wing. He felt that if he stayed calm and looked, he could see how things should fit together.
sentences.grammar: ‘if he relaxed ..., he could see’ is ‘if + past, could + verb’: what might happen; ‘he’d had’ (past perfect) means a time before that moment.

sentences.context: As if Glory’s nothing more than a tapestry to hang on the wall
sentences.simple: It is as if Glory is only a cloth picture to hang on the wall. She is not a dragon with feelings, ideas, a destiny and friends who care about her.
sentences.grammar: ‘As if’ starts an unreal comparison (Glory is not a tapestry); ‘nothing more than’ means ‘only’; ‘not a dragon with ...’ lists what Glory really is.

sentences.context: Clay had been scanning the prisoners around the circle since spotting Starflight
sentences.simple: Clay had been looking carefully at the prisoners around the circle since he saw Starflight. But he could not see any tiny gold dragons or unusual colors.
sentences.grammar: ‘had been scanning’ (past perfect continuous) shows he kept looking up to that time; ‘since spotting’ = ‘since he spotted’.

sentences.context: so if I put one of you into it, it would be very thoughtful
sentences.simple: But I also promised my people that today’s fight would be exciting. So if I put one of you in it, it would be very kind of you if you could win.
sentences.grammar: ‘so if I put ..., it would be ... if you could win’ is a ‘what if’ sentence (if + present, would + verb); ‘thoughtful’ means kind to others, and the queen says it as a cruel joke.

sentences.context: Time to find out if he did have a monster inside
sentences.simple: It was time to find out if he really had a monster inside him. And if so, was it the useful kind, or the kind that would make him hate himself later, or both?
sentences.grammar: ‘if’ here means ‘whether’; ‘did have’ uses ‘did’ for stress (is it really true?); ‘the kind that would make him hate himself’ is a ‘that’ clause telling which kind.

sentences.context: If he attacked now, he could surprise the other dragon and maybe even win
sentences.simple: If he attacked now, he could surprise the other dragon and maybe even win.
sentences.grammar: ‘If he attacked now, he could surprise’ is ‘if + past, could + verb’: a ‘what if’ idea about something he might do; ‘maybe even win’ adds one more possibility.

sentences.context: but to be right underneath the dying dragon, his screams piercing Clay’s ears
sentences.simple: The dragon that Peril had killed had screamed with this kind of pain. But it was much worse to be right under the dying dragon, with his screams hurting Clay’s ears.
sentences.grammar: ‘to be right underneath ...’ is the subject of the sentence; ‘his screams piercing’ is a short phrase that adds what was happening.

sentences.context: as if he were trying to get close enough to see their faces from
sentences.simple: Osprey stretched his neck toward the queen and then toward Kestrel. It was as if he were trying to get close enough to see their faces from his rock.
sentences.grammar: ‘as if he were trying’ uses ‘were’ to say how it looked, not what was true; ‘close enough to + verb’ says how close he wanted to be.

sentences.context: Upon hatching, it turned out to hold twin dragonets
sentences.simple: When the egg hatched, it turned out to hold two dragonets, twins.
sentences.grammar: ‘Upon + -ing’ means ‘when’ (when it hatched); ‘turned out to + verb’ means it was found in the end to be so.

sentences.context: In the confusion and the dark, they each thought the other had unclipped
sentences.simple: In the confusion and the dark, each of them thought the other one had unclipped that leg. They flew him down to the sand without noticing their mistake.
sentences.grammar: ‘thought the other had unclipped’ (past perfect) is a belief about an earlier action; ‘without catching their mistake’ means ‘without noticing it’.

sentences.context: but her claws and teeth were stained red from all the blood she had
sentences.simple: She wore no jewels or chain mail. But her claws and teeth were stained red with all the blood she had spilled. A bad scar was burned along her left side, below the wing.
sentences.grammar: ‘were stained’ is passive; ‘all the blood she had shed’ is a clause with no ‘that’, and ‘had shed’ (past perfect) is earlier.

sentences.context: stood awkwardly as if they would rather be charging into battle
sentences.simple: The SandWings looked rough and common next to the SkyWings. Many of them stood awkwardly, as if they would rather be charging into battle than making polite conversation at a party.
sentences.grammar: ‘would rather + verb ... than + verb’ says what they prefer (‘be charging’ rather than ‘making’); ‘as if’ tells how they looked, not what was sure.

sentences.context: trying to look as if he was perfectly comfortable in the air
sentences.simple: Vermilion swooped over the crowd. He tried to look completely comfortable in the air, not on the sand where he usually did his announcing.
sentences.grammar: ‘as if he was comfortable’ tells how he wanted to look, not how he felt; ‘instead of on the sands’ gives the other place; ‘where he usually did his announcing’ is a ‘where’ clause.

sentences.context: her back turned to the SeaWing corpse, which was already beginning to smell
sentences.simple: Tsunami was still standing in the arena, with her back turned to the dead SeaWing. It was already beginning to smell of dead fish.
sentences.grammar: ‘her back turned’ is a short phrase meaning ‘with her back turned’; ‘which was already beginning’ is a ‘which’ clause about the body.

sentences.context: as if he wasn’t entirely sure she wouldn’t snap and kill him
sentences.simple: Tsunami looked a bit scarier than usual, and Starflight clawed the sand nervously. It looked as if he was not completely sure she would not snap and kill him.
sentences.grammar: ‘wasn’t entirely sure she wouldn’t’ has two ‘n’t’: it means he thought she might; ‘as if’ tells how it looked.

sentences.context: as if they were drawing in the sunlight
sentences.simple: Her wing scales shimmered as if they were taking in the sunlight. Then the purple color started to break up, like water being poured into paint.
sentences.grammar: ‘as if they were drawing in’ compares the look to something else (‘drawing in’ means ‘taking in’); ‘being poured’ is a passive -ing phrase.

sentences.context: One IceWing had been dropped at the base of the cliff
sentences.simple: One IceWing had been dropped at the bottom of the cliff, not far from the waterfall. The spray made a small rainbow over his torn silver wings and bloody scales.
sentences.grammar: ‘had been dropped’ is passive past perfect: someone did it before; the doer is not named.

sentences.context: as if a dragon had punched through the mud in a rage
sentences.simple: Next to the lake was a lopsided mound with a hole falling apart near the top. It looked as if, at some point, a dragon had punched through the mud in anger.
sentences.grammar: ‘as if a dragon had punched’ uses the past perfect to guess about something that happened before; it is not sure.

sentences.context: it still hurt worse than anything he’d ever felt
sentences.simple: Clay could see that she was not trying to be mean. But it still hurt worse than anything he had ever felt. It hurt more than Kestrel’s attacks, the IceWing’s claws in his back, seeing Sunny in a cage, or knowing Peril had betrayed them.
sentences.grammar: ‘worse than anything he’d ever felt’ (past perfect) compares with all of his life before; ‘more than ...’ adds a list.

sentences.context: If she’d lived, she could have told him how things were in the Mud
sentences.simple: If she had lived, she could have told him how things were in the Mud Kingdom. That would have saved him a lot of useless dreaming.
sentences.grammar: ‘If she’d lived, she could have told’ is the third conditional: if + past perfect, could have + past participle. It talks about the past that did not happen: she did not live.

sentences.context: as if she would rather die than replace them with unsibs
sentences.simple: Pheasant looked at the others, Umber, Sora and Marsh, as if she would rather die than replace them with unsibs. Unsibs were not her own brothers and sisters.
sentences.grammar: ‘would rather die than + verb’ means she strongly does not want to; ‘who weren’t her own brothers and sisters’ is a ‘who’ clause.

think about.meaning: To have something in your thoughts; to consider it.
think about.example: Clay didn’t like to think about that.

go on.meaning: To continue, especially to keep talking after a stop.
go on.example: I’ve been queen for ages and ages,” Sunny went on.

come on.meaning: Words you say to ask someone to go with you, go faster, or try harder.

let out.meaning: To make a sound, such as a roar or a yell. Also: to set something free.
let out.example: He let out another yowl of pain

out of the way.meaning: Not in the path of someone or something; to the side.
out of the way.example: Sunny darted out of the way

think of.meaning: To have something in your mind; to imagine it, remember it, or find an idea.

let go.example: grabbed the chain and let go at once

come back.example: That’s why she didn’t come back for you.”

step back.meaning: To move a short way backward.
step back.example: He stepped back and swung his tail

pick up.meaning: To lift something up. Also: to get or collect something.
pick up.example: scrolls picked up by the Talons of Peace

take care of.meaning: To look after, or to deal with something.
take care of.example: But I can take care of that for you.”

fight back.meaning: To defend yourself against someone who attacks you. Also: to hold back a strong feeling.

by the way.meaning: Words you use to add something extra to what you are saying.
by the way.example: Also, by the way, most of the SandWings

find out.meaning: To learn something that you did not know.
find out.example: we’ll find out what the fuss is

get away.meaning: To get free from someone or something; to go away from a place or a person.
get away.example: she still might get away from you

come true.meaning: To happen as hoped or said.
come true.example: to make the prophecy come true

hold on.meaning: To keep holding tight. Also: to last through a hard time.
hold on.example: He only had to hold on that long

all at once.meaning: At the same time. Also: suddenly.
all at once.example: Sunny and Glory all at once

run away.meaning: To go away fast from danger or trouble; to leave a place.
run away.example: Let’s run away now and worry about that later

shut up.meaning: To stop talking. It is not a kind thing to say.

turn out.meaning: To be found, in the end, to be a certain way.
turn out.example: it turned out to hold twin dragonets

burst into.meaning: To suddenly start to be something, such as flames. Also: to rush suddenly into a place.

keep going.example: Don’t keep going if it’s too dangerous.”

wake up.example: relief to wake up after dark

stay away.meaning: To not go near someone or something.
stay away.example: supposed to stay away from the arena

figure out.meaning: To find the answer to something by thinking.
figure out.example: figure out what was broken, and fix it

no matter.meaning: Words that mean ‘it does not change anything’: no matter how much, where or which.
no matter.example: no matter how much she pretended she didn’t care

calm down.meaning: To become quiet and not upset; to make someone do this.

give up.meaning: To stop trying; to stop doing something.
give up.example: would give up and fly away
